title: Introduction, behavioral formalisms and Petri nets

cards.question: What is process mining, in one sentence?
cards.answer: A family of techniques that use event data recorded by information systems to discover, monitor and improve real processes.
distractors: A family of techniques that use manually drawn process models to predict future sales figures.
A data-mining method that clusters customers by purchase behavior.
A software-engineering practice for converting source code into executable process models.

cards.question: Why is process mining described as the missing link between data science and process science?
cards.answer: Data science is data-centric but largely process-agnostic, while process science is model-centric but often disconnected from data. Process mining connects event data with process models.
distractors: Data science focuses only on models, while process science focuses only on raw data storage.
Process mining replaces both disciplines with a single fully automated approach.
Data science studies human workers, while process science studies machines.

cards.question: What are the three main types of process mining techniques?
cards.answer: Discovery, conformance checking and enhancement.
distractors: Discovery, classification and regression.
Modelling, simulation and deployment.
Extraction, transformation and loading.

cards.question: What are the input and output of process discovery?
cards.answer: The input is an event log; the output is a process model.
distractors: The input is a process model; the output is an event log.
The input is a process model and an event log; the output is a list of deviations.
The input is an event log; the output is a set of business rules written in natural language.

cards.question: What are the input and output of conformance checking?
cards.answer: The input is an event log and a process model; the output is diagnostics on where and how the behavior in the log and in the model deviate.
distractors: The input is only an event log; the output is a newly discovered process model.
The input is only a process model; the output is a simulated event log.
The input is an event log; the output is an improved model with performance annotations.

cards.question: What does the enhancement type of process mining do?
cards.answer: It uses information from the event log to improve or extend an existing process model, for example by adding performance or bottleneck information.
distractors: It discovers a process model from scratch using only an event log.
It checks whether a log perfectly replays on a model and reports deviations.
It converts a process model into executable code for a workflow engine.

cards.question: What is the difference between process discovery and conformance checking?
cards.answer: Discovery constructs a model from a log without prior model; conformance checking compares an existing model with a log to find deviations.
distractors: Discovery compares a model with a log; conformance checking constructs a model from a log.
Discovery works on models only; conformance checking works on logs only.
Discovery changes the model using log information; conformance checking changes the log using the model.

cards.question: What is the difference between conformance checking and enhancement?
cards.answer: Conformance checking measures how well model and log fit and reports deviations; enhancement changes or extends the model using the log, for example to add performance data or repair it.
distractors: Conformance checking improves the model; enhancement only reports deviations.
Conformance checking needs no log; enhancement needs no model.
They are the same technique with different names.

cards.question: A company has an event log but no process model and wants to know how its process really runs. Which type of process mining applies?
cards.answer: Process discovery.
distractors: Conformance checking.
Enhancement.
Process simulation.

cards.question: A hospital has a prescribed treatment model and wants to know whether staff follow it in practice. Which type of process mining applies?
cards.answer: Conformance checking.
distractors: Process discovery.
Enhancement by adding new activities.
Data cleaning.

cards.question: A company wants to annotate its existing process model with waiting times to find bottlenecks. Which type of process mining applies?
cards.answer: Enhancement (extension), using timestamps from the event log.
distractors: Process discovery.
Conformance checking.
Event log generation.

cards.question: What is an event log?
cards.answer: A collection of recorded events, each referring to a case, an activity and a point in time, produced by executions of a process.
distractors: A manually written description of how a process should be executed.
A graph of places and transitions describing allowed behavior.
A table of aggregated yearly performance indicators.

cards.question: Which attributes are the minimum needed for each event in process mining?
cards.answer: A case identifier, an activity name and a timestamp (or an ordering).
distractors: A resource name, a cost and a location.
A transition name, a place and a marking.
A model identifier, a version and an author.

cards.question: What does the case identifier of an event tell you?
cards.answer: Which process instance (case) the event belongs to.
distractors: Which resource executed the event.
Which model the event conforms to.
How long the activity took.

cards.question: What is a trace in the context of an event log?
cards.answer: The sequence of activities of one case, ordered by their occurrence.
distractors: The set of all activities of the whole log, without ordering.
A path from the initial to the final place of a Petri net, including its markings.
The list of resources involved in all cases.

cards.question: Why is the order of events within a case important for process mining?
cards.answer: Control-flow relations between activities (what follows what) can only be derived from the order in which events occurred.
distractors: It is required only to compute the number of cases.
It only matters for anonymizing resources.
It is irrelevant, since only activity names matter.

cards.question: What additional information beyond case, activity and time is often found in event logs and enables other perspectives?
cards.answer: Resources (who executed an activity) and data attributes such as costs or amounts.
distractors: The source code of the information system.
The Petri net marking at each moment.
The full process model used by the company.

cards.question: What are the three main perspectives of a process model?
cards.answer: Control flow (ordering of activities), data (information used and produced) and resources (who performs the activities).
distractors: Cost, quality and risk.
Syntax, semantics and pragmatics.
Input, process and output.

cards.question: Which perspective does a Petri net primarily capture?
cards.answer: The control-flow perspective.
distractors: The resource perspective.
The data perspective.
The organizational hierarchy.

cards.question: Name common purposes of process modelling.
cards.answer: Understanding and documenting a process, communicating about it, analyzing and verifying it, simulating it, and configuring or executing it in a system.
distractors: Only generating source code from diagrams.
Only providing legal evidence for audits.
Only calculating employee salaries.

cards.question: What is the definition of a business process by Hammer and Champy (1993)?
cards.answer: A collection of activities that takes one or more kinds of input and creates an output that is of value to the customer.
distractors: A fixed sequence of IT system calls that never changes.
A set of rules describing the hierarchy of a company.
A collection of data tables describing customers and products.

cards.question: What is a typical emphasis of Davenport's (1992) definition of a process?
cards.answer: A specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and clearly identified inputs and outputs.
distractors: A statistical distribution of arrival times of customers.
An unordered set of tasks performed by one department.
A static database schema of business entities.

cards.question: What is a process-aware information system (PAIS)?
cards.answer: An information system that manages and executes operational processes involving people, applications and data, driven by explicit process models.
distractors: A system that only stores documents without any notion of process.
A spreadsheet in which users record their own tasks.
A system that mines logs offline and has no execution capabilities.

cards.question: What is the role of a workflow engine in a process-aware information system?
cards.answer: It executes process models by creating cases, enabling tasks, and assigning work to people or applications in the right order.
distractors: It discovers process models from event logs.
It stores the event log in a data warehouse.
It trains predictive models on historical data.

cards.question: What is the idea of process orchestration?
cards.answer: A central process model coordinates the execution of tasks and the interaction among systems and people.
distractors: Every system independently decides what to do next without any central model.
Tasks are executed in random order to balance workload.
Processes are discovered automatically after execution.

cards.question: What is process-based integration?
cards.answer: Connecting existing applications and services by an explicit process model that determines the order in which they are invoked.
distractors: Merging two companies' databases into one schema.
Replacing all applications with one monolithic system.
Integrating event logs from different cases into one trace.

cards.question: What distinguishes human interaction workflows from system-to-system process orchestration?
cards.answer: In human interaction workflows, people perform tasks (for example via worklists), while orchestration mostly coordinates automated services.
distractors: Human workflows contain no control flow.
Human workflows never produce events.
Human workflows are executed without any process model.

cards.question: Why can event logs of a process-aware system differ from those of a system without process support?
cards.answer: Process-aware systems explicitly record cases and activities, so events are easy to relate to process instances; other systems may require extensive reconstruction of cases.
distractors: Process-aware systems never record timestamps.
Systems without process support always produce cleaner logs.
Event logs can only be obtained from process-aware systems.

cards.question: What is a Petri net, formally, as a bipartite structure?
cards.answer: A triple (P, T, F) of places, transitions and a flow relation F ⊆ (P×T) ∪ (T×P), with P and T disjoint.
distractors: A tuple (S, s0, L, R) of states, initial state, labels and transition relation.
A pair (V, E) of vertices and undirected edges.
A triple (P, T, M) of places, transitions and markings.

cards.question: In a Petri net, what do circles and rectangles typically represent?
cards.answer: Circles represent places and rectangles represent transitions.
distractors: Circles represent transitions and rectangles represent places.
Circles represent tokens and rectangles represent markings.
Circles represent resources and rectangles represent cases.

cards.question: Why is a Petri net called bipartite?
cards.answer: Arcs only connect places to transitions or transitions to places, never two nodes of the same kind.
distractors: It always has exactly two places.
It is made of two separate subnets.
Every transition has exactly two arcs.

cards.question: What is the preset •t of a transition t?
cards.answer: The set of input places of t, that is, places p with (p,t) ∈ F.
distractors: The set of output places of t.
The set of transitions that fire before t.
The set of tokens currently on t.

cards.question: What is the postset t• of a transition t?
cards.answer: The set of output places of t, that is, places p with (t,p) ∈ F.
distractors: The set of input places of t.
The set of transitions enabled after t fires.
The set of tokens produced by all transitions.

cards.question: For a place p, what do •p and p• denote?
cards.answer: •p is the set of transitions with an arc into p; p• is the set of transitions with an arc out of p.
distractors: •p is the set of tokens on p; p• is the capacity of p.
•p is the set of output places; p• the set of input places.
•p and p• both denote the number of tokens in p.

cards.question: What is a marking of a Petri net?
cards.answer: A distribution of tokens over the places, that is, the state of the net (a function or multiset over P).
distractors: The set of transitions that have fired so far.
The labelling of transitions with activity names.
A path from the initial to the final place.

cards.question: When is a transition t enabled in marking M?
cards.answer: When every input place of t contains at least one token in M.
distractors: When at least one input place of t contains a token.
When all output places of t are empty.
When the net is in its initial marking.

cards.question: What happens when an enabled transition fires?
cards.answer: One token is consumed from each input place and one token is produced in each output place.
distractors: All tokens in the net are moved to the output places.
One token is consumed from one input place and produced in one output place.
The transition is removed from the net.

cards.question: Is the firing of a transition atomic in a Petri net?
cards.answer: Yes; consuming and producing tokens happens as one indivisible step.
distractors: No; tokens are consumed first and produced after a delay.
No; each input token is consumed in a separate step.
Only if the transition has a single input place.

cards.question: If two transitions are enabled in the same marking, which one fires?
cards.answer: Either one: the choice is non-deterministic, and the semantics do not prescribe any preference.
distractors: The one with the lowest index always fires.
Both fire simultaneously.
The one with more input places fires.

cards.question: What is a Petri net system?
cards.answer: A Petri net N together with an initial marking M0, written (N, M0).
distractors: A Petri net with a final marking only.
A set of Petri nets executed in parallel.
A Petri net whose places have capacities.

cards.question: What is the difference between a Petri net and a Petri net system?
cards.answer: A Petri net is only the static structure (P, T, F); a Petri net system adds an initial marking and thus has behavior.
distractors: A Petri net has tokens, while a system has none.
A Petri net is bipartite, while a system is not.
A Petri net is finite, while a system is infinite.

cards.question: What does it mean for a marking M' to be reachable from M0?
cards.answer: There is a sequence of transition firings, starting in M0, that leads to M'.
distractors: M' contains at least as many tokens as M0.
M' and M0 share at least one marked place.
M' is obtained by adding one token to M0.

cards.question: What is the reachability graph of a Petri net system?
cards.answer: A transition system whose states are the reachable markings and whose edges are firings of enabled transitions.
distractors: A graph showing which places can reach which other places by arcs.
The same graph as the Petri net itself.
A list of all transitions never enabled.

cards.question: Why can a Petri net with few nodes still have a large reachability graph?
cards.answer: Concurrency and choice produce many different token distributions, so states can multiply (state explosion).
distractors: Because each place stores arbitrarily many labels.
Because every transition appears several times in the graph.
Because reachability graphs include unreachable markings.

cards.question: What is the typical multiset notation for a marking with one token in p1 and two tokens in p2?
distractors: {p1, p2} as a plain set.
(1, 2) without place names.
p1 + p2 as a sum of transition names.

cards.question: How does a Petri net model a parallel split (AND-split)?
cards.answer: A transition with several output places: when it fires, tokens are produced in all of them, enabling concurrent branches.
distractors: A place with several output transitions.
A transition with a single output place.
Two transitions with the same label.

cards.question: How does a Petri net model an exclusive choice (XOR-split)?
cards.answer: A place with several outgoing transitions: the token can be consumed by only one of them.
distractors: A transition with several output places.
A transition with several input places.
A place with several tokens and one outgoing transition.

cards.question: How does a Petri net model synchronization (AND-join)?
cards.answer: A transition with several input places, enabled only when all of them hold a token.
distractors: A place with several incoming transitions.
A place with several outgoing transitions.
A transition with a single input place.

cards.question: What is the difference between choice and concurrency in a Petri net?
cards.answer: In a choice, firing one enabled transition disables the others (they compete for a token); in concurrency, enabled transitions can all fire independently.
distractors: Choice means tokens are created; concurrency means tokens are destroyed.
Choice occurs only with transitions; concurrency only with places.
They are two names for the same structure.

cards.question: What is a workflow net (WF-net)?
cards.answer: A Petri net with a single source place i, a single sink place o, and every node on a path from i to o.
distractors: A Petri net with exactly one transition.
A Petri net in which every place has exactly one token.
A Petri net with no choices and no concurrency.

cards.question: What are the structural requirements on the initial place i of a workflow net?
cards.answer: It has no incoming arcs (•i = ∅).
distractors: It has no outgoing arcs.
It has exactly one incoming and one outgoing arc.
It must contain two tokens initially.

cards.question: What are the structural requirements on the final place o of a workflow net?
cards.answer: It has no outgoing arcs (o• = ∅).
distractors: It has no incoming arcs.
It has exactly one outgoing arc to the initial place.
It must always hold the only token in the initial marking.

cards.question: What is the initial marking of a workflow net, typically?
cards.answer: A single token in the initial place i, representing a new case.
distractors: A token in every place.
A token in the final place o.
No tokens at all.

cards.question: Why must every node of a workflow net lie on a path from i to o?
cards.answer: It ensures that no part of the net is disconnected from the process start and end, so every element is relevant to the case's execution.
distractors: It guarantees that the net has no choices.
It ensures all transitions fire at least once per case.
It makes the net acyclic.

cards.question: What does adding a transition t* from o to i do to a workflow net?
cards.answer: It makes the net strongly connected; a workflow net is a WF-net exactly when this extended net is strongly connected.
distractors: It makes the net acyclic.
It turns the net into a transition system.
It removes the final place from the net.

cards.question: What does 'strongly connected' mean for a net?
cards.answer: There is a directed path from every node to every other node.
distractors: Every node has at least one token.
The underlying undirected graph is connected.
All transitions are enabled at the same time.

cards.question: Is the following a valid workflow net: a net with two disconnected places that have no path from i to o?
cards.answer: No; every node must be on a path from i to o, so disconnected nodes violate the definition.
distractors: Yes, extra places are always allowed.
Yes, as long as the net is bipartite.
Yes, if the extra places have no tokens.

cards.question: What is a trace in the behavioral formalism sense?
cards.answer: A finite sequence of activities (labels) describing one possible execution.
distractors: An unordered set of states of a process.
A single transition of a transition system.
A numeric measure of process performance.

cards.question: What is the empty trace ε?
cards.answer: The trace with no activities; it is the trace of a process that has not yet executed anything.
distractors: A trace containing a single unnamed activity.
A trace that can never occur.
A trace containing all possible activities.

cards.question: Why can a set of traces be insufficient to capture the 'moment of choice' of a process?
cards.answer: Sets of traces only list the sequences of activities, not the states in which choices are made.
distractors: Traces contain too much state information.
Traces cannot represent sequences of length greater than one.
Traces are only defined for Petri nets.

cards.question: What is a labelled transition system (LTS)?
cards.answer: A tuple (S, s0, L, R) of states, an initial state, labels, and a labelled transition relation R ⊆ S × L × S.
distractors: A tuple (P, T, F) of places, transitions and flow relation.
A tuple (i, o, T) of initial place, final place and transitions.
A tuple (E, C, A) of events, cases and activities.

cards.question: What is the advantage of an LTS for representing behavior?
cards.answer: It gives a finite representation of a possibly infinite set of traces and exposes the states in which choices are made.
distractors: It always has fewer states than a Petri net.
It removes the need for an initial state.
It records the resources behind each activity.

cards.question: What role do the labels of an LTS play?
cards.answer: They name the actions (activities) that cause transitions between states.
distractors: They name the states of the system.
They give the number of tokens in each state.
They denote the initial state.

cards.question: What are the two ingredients of the relation R in an LTS (S, s0, L, R)?
cards.answer: Triples (s, l, s') meaning that from state s the system can move to state s' by performing label l.
distractors: Pairs of states without any labels.
Pairs (l, l') of consecutive labels.
Pairs (s, token count).

cards.question: What does it mean for two process models to be trace equivalent?
cards.answer: They have exactly the same set of traces.
distractors: They have the same number of states.
They have the same graph structure.
They have the same set of complete traces and different traces.

cards.question: What does it mean for two models to be complete-trace equivalent?
cards.answer: They have exactly the same set of complete traces, that is, runs that end in a final state.
distractors: They have the same set of prefixes of traces only.
They have the same graph, up to node renaming.
They have the same number of final states.

cards.question: What is the difference between trace equivalence and complete-trace equivalence?
cards.answer: Trace equivalence compares all possible partial executions (prefixes); complete-trace equivalence compares only the executions that terminate in a final state, so it distinguishes models that stop at different points.
distractors: Trace equivalence compares labels; complete-trace equivalence compares states.
Trace equivalence is stronger than complete-trace equivalence.
They coincide for every pair of models.

cards.question: Two models can be trace equivalent but not complete-trace equivalent. How is this possible?
cards.answer: They allow the same prefixes, but they differ in which of these sequences are allowed to end the process.
distractors: They have different initial states.
They have different label sets.
This is impossible, since complete traces are a subset of traces.

cards.question: Model A: a then b or c. Model B: a then (b or c) via two different a-branches, one followed by b and one by c. Are they trace equivalent?
cards.answer: Yes; both have the traces ε, a, ab and ac, even though the moment of choice differs.
distractors: No, because B has more states than A.
No, because B allows trace ab only.
No, because A cannot execute a.

cards.question: What is a limitation of trace equivalence?
cards.answer: It ignores the moment at which a choice is made, so models with different choice structures can be considered equal.
distractors: It can only compare Petri nets.
It requires the models to be acyclic.
It distinguishes models that behave identically.

cards.question: Why does behavioral equivalence focus on behavior and not on structure?
cards.answer: Process models describe behavior, so two models with different structure can still allow the same behavior and should then be considered equivalent.
distractors: Because structure cannot be formalized.
Because structurally different models always behave differently.
Because behavior is easier to draw.

cards.question: Besides behavior, what other aspects can be used to assess equivalence of process models?
cards.answer: Model structure and the business semantics of activities.
distractors: The color and layout of the diagrams.
The programming language used to execute them.
The number of employees involved.

cards.question: For the set T = {ε, a, ab, ac}, which of the following traces could be a trace of a model with that trace set?
cards.answer: ac
distractors: ba
abc
aa

cards.question: How can a Petri net system be viewed as an LTS?
cards.answer: Take the reachable markings as states, the initial marking as s0, transition names (or labels) as labels, and firing as the relation R, which gives the reachability graph.
distractors: Take the places as states and the tokens as labels.
Take the transitions as states and the arcs as labels.
It cannot be viewed as an LTS because it is concurrent.

cards.question: Why do event logs generally contain only a sample of the behavior of a process?
cards.answer: A log records only the cases that actually occurred, so rare or not-yet-observed behavior may be missing even though the process allows it.
distractors: Logs contain all possible traces of the process model.
Logs record only the first event of each case.
Logs are generated by simulation only.
